decks.title: Magnetism and Matter — Part 1: The bar magnet as a magnetic dipole
goals: Describe the field lines of a bar magnet and compare them with electric field lines
Explain why a bar magnet behaves like an equivalent solenoid
Describe the field of a magnetic dipole on its axis and equatorial line, and the torque on it in a uniform field (qualitatively)

slides.heading: Magnetism and Matter
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the bar magnet seen as a tiny current loop: its field lines, its field at different points and its behaviour in a uniform field.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: bar magnet, field lines, equivalent solenoid, axial and equatorial field, torque in a field

slides.narration: A fridge magnet, a compass needle and a motor’s magnet all behave in the same way. In this part we look at the bar magnet as a magnetic dipole. We describe its field lines, see why it behaves exactly like a small current-carrying solenoid, compare its field at different points, and find out what a uniform field does to it.

slides.heading: Properties of a bar magnet
slides.body_md: A freely suspended bar magnet settles roughly north–south. Its two ends are its **north (N)** and **south (S)** poles.
bullets: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
Breaking a magnet gives two smaller magnets, each with N and S: **isolated poles (monopoles) are not found**.
The **magnetic moment** $\vec m$ points from S to N inside the magnet (unit A m²).

rows: Attraction is strongest near the ends
N and S always come together
Each piece is a complete magnet

visual.alt: Table of bar-magnet properties: directive, poles, poles in pairs and breaking into complete magnets

slides.narration: Hang a bar magnet freely and it turns until it points roughly north and south. The end pointing north is called its north pole. Iron filings cling most strongly near the two ends. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. And however many times you break a magnet, every piece has both a north and a south pole: no one has found an isolated magnetic pole.

slides.heading: Field lines of a bar magnet
slides.body_md: Magnetic field lines form **continuous closed loops**: outside the magnet they run from N to S, and inside from S to N.
bullets: The tangent gives the direction of $\vec B$; crowding shows strength.
Field lines never cross.
They do not start or end anywhere, because there are no monopoles.

visual.alt: Closed field lines of a bar magnet running outside from N to S and inside from S to N
visual.caption: Traced numerically from the equivalent solenoid (Biot–Savart over its circular turns).

slides.narration: Sprinkle iron filings round a bar magnet and they trace out its field lines. Outside the magnet the lines run from the north pole round to the south pole. Unlike electric field lines, they do not stop there: they carry on inside the magnet from south back to north, so every line is a closed loop. This is the picture of a magnetic dipole.

slides.heading: Magnetic and electric field lines compared
slides.body_md: Both describe a field, but with one key difference:
columns:
**Electric field lines (dipole)**

- Start on + charges, end on − charges
- Never form closed loops
- Between the charges they point from + to −

**Magnetic field lines (bar magnet)**

- No start or end: closed loops
- Inside the magnet they run S → N
- Net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero

visual.alt: Closed field lines of a bar magnet running outside from N to S and inside from S to N
visual.caption: Traced numerically from the equivalent solenoid (Biot–Savart over its circular turns).

slides.narration: Electric field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges. Magnetic field lines have nowhere to begin or end, because there are no magnetic charges, so they always close on themselves. A consequence is that the total magnetic flux out of any closed surface is zero: every line that leaves also comes back in. Outside the magnets the two dipole patterns look alike.

slides.body_md: Decide whether the statement is true or false.
slides.narration: Think about where magnetic field lines could begin or end, if there are no isolated magnetic poles.

slides.heading: The bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid
slides.body_md:
A current-carrying solenoid produces the **same field pattern** as a bar magnet: its end where the current looks anticlockwise is a north pole. Its magnetic moment is
$$m = NIA$$
for $N$ turns of area $A$ carrying current $I$. In a magnet, the circulating electrons in its atoms play the part of the turns.

visual.alt: Field lines of a short solenoid, the same pattern as a bar magnet
visual.caption: Same calculation as the bar-magnet figure, with the turns drawn.

slides.narration: Compare this picture with the bar magnet. A short solenoid carrying a current makes exactly the same pattern of closed field lines, with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other. Its magnetic moment is N I A. Inside a real magnet, electrons circulating and spinning in the atoms act like countless tiny current loops all lined up, which is why a magnet behaves like a solenoid.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: matching a magnet with a solenoid
slides.body_md: A solenoid of 400 turns, each of area 2.0 cm², carries 1.5 A. What is its magnetic moment? A bar magnet with the same moment would produce the same field far away.
bullets: Step 1 — $A = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}$ m².
Step 2 — $m = NIA = 400 \times 1.5 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-4} = 0.12$ A m².
Step 3 — direction: along the axis, towards the end where the current appears anticlockwise (the N end).

visual.alt: Field lines of a short solenoid, the same pattern as a bar magnet
visual.caption: Same calculation as the bar-magnet figure, with the turns drawn.

slides.narration: Convert two square centimetres to two times ten to the minus four square metre. Multiply turns, current and area to get a magnetic moment of zero point one two ampere square metre, along the axis towards the end that acts as a north pole. Far from it, a bar magnet with this same moment would produce an identical field, which is what equivalent means.

slides.heading: Field of a bar magnet at axial and equatorial points
slides.body_md: By analogy with the electric dipole (treated qualitatively), at a large distance $r$:
bullets: **Axial point:** field along $\vec m$, size $\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{2m}{r^3}$.
**Equatorial point:** field opposite to $\vec m$, size $\dfrac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\dfrac{m}{r^3}$ — half the axial value at the same distance.
Both fall as $1/r^3$, much faster than the field of a single pole would.

slides.narration: The field of a bar magnet far away has the same shape as that of an electric dipole, with mu nought over four pi in place of one over four pi epsilon nought and m in place of p. On the axis the field points along the magnetic moment; on the equatorial line it points the opposite way and is half as strong at the same distance. Both weaken as the cube of the distance.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: comparing fields by ratio
slides.body_md: A short bar magnet produces a field $B$ at a point on its axis 20 cm away. Find, qualitatively and by ratio, the field (a) on its equatorial line 20 cm away, (b) on its axis 40 cm away.
bullets: Step 1 — same distance: equatorial field is half the axial field, so (a) $B/2$, pointing opposite to $\vec m$.
Step 2 — doubling the distance divides a $1/r^3$ field by $2^3 = 8$, so (b) $B/8$, along $\vec m$.
Check — the field 40 cm away on the equator would be $B/16$.

slides.heading: A bar magnet in a uniform field
slides.body_md:
In a uniform field the forces on the two poles are equal and opposite: **no net force**, but a **couple**:
$$\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B,\qquad \tau = mB\sin\theta$$
It turns the magnet to line up with $\vec B$ — which is how a compass needle works.

slides.narration: Place a bar magnet at an angle in a uniform field. Its north pole is pushed along the field and its south pole the opposite way, with equal forces, so the magnet does not move off, but it turns. The torque is m B sine theta, exactly as for a current loop. It turns the magnet into line with the field, and that is all a compass needle is doing when it points north.

slides.heading: Equilibrium and oscillation
slides.body_md: Like the current loop and the electric dipole:
bullets: **Stable** equilibrium: $\vec m$ along $\vec B$ ($\theta = 0$), lowest potential energy $-mB$.
**Unstable** equilibrium: $\vec m$ opposite to $\vec B$ ($\theta = 180^\circ$), highest energy $+mB$.
Displaced slightly from the stable position, a freely pivoted magnet **oscillates** about the field direction; a stronger field makes it oscillate faster.

visual.alt: Table of orientations of a magnet in a field with torque, energy and type of equilibrium

slides.narration: A magnet pointing along the field is in stable equilibrium: nudge it and the torque pulls it back, so it swings to and fro about the field direction. Pointing exactly against the field it is balanced but unstable. The potential energy is lowest, minus m B, when aligned and highest, plus m B, when reversed. In a stronger field the restoring torque is larger, so the oscillations are faster.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: torque on a magnet
slides.body_md: A bar magnet of moment 0.12 A m² is placed at $30^\circ$ to a uniform field of 0.050 T. Find the torque on it. In which position would the torque be largest?
bullets: Step 1 — $\tau = mB\sin\theta = 0.12 \times 0.050 \times 0.5 = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}$ N m.
Step 2 — the torque is largest when the magnet is at right angles to the field ($\sin 90^\circ = 1$): $6.0 \times 10^{-3}$ N m.
Step 3 — the torque turns the magnet towards the field direction; the net force is zero.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key ideas:

rows: Closed loops: outside N → S, inside S → N
Poles always in pairs; net flux through a closed surface is 0
Axial $\propto 2m/r^3$ along m; equatorial $\propto m/r^3$ opposite to m
$\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B$; no net force; stable when aligned

visual.alt: Summary table of field lines, monopoles, equivalent solenoid, far field and behaviour in a uniform field

slides.narration: To sum up: a bar magnet is a magnetic dipole. Its field lines are closed loops, running outside from north to south and inside from south to north, because there are no isolated poles. It is equivalent to a solenoid with moment N I A. Far away its field falls as one over r cubed, twice as strong on the axis as on the equator. In a uniform field it feels a torque m cross B but no net force.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: Draw field lines as **closed loops** with arrows, including inside the magnet (S → N).
Ratio questions: $1/r^3$ for distance, factor 2 between axial and equatorial points.
Say “no net force but a torque” for a magnet in a uniform field.
The treatment is qualitative: explain with the solenoid analogy rather than pole formulas.

visual.alt: Table of how the far field of a bar magnet changes with distance, position and moment

slides.narration: In field-line diagrams, examiners look for closed loops with arrows, continuing inside the magnet from south to north. Use ratios for comparison questions: a factor of eight for doubling the distance, and a factor of two between axial and equatorial points. For a magnet in a uniform field, always say there is a torque but no net force.

decks.title: Magnetism and Matter — Part 2: Magnetic properties of materials
goals: Define magnetisation, magnetic intensity, susceptibility and relative permeability
Classify materials as diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic, with examples
Explain the effect of temperature on magnetic properties (Curie law, Curie temperature)

slides.heading: Magnetic properties of materials
slides.body_md: Part 2 — why iron is pulled strongly into a magnetic field, aluminium only slightly, and bismuth is pushed out.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: magnetisation, magnetic intensity, susceptibility and permeability, three classes of material, effect of temperature

slides.narration: Every material responds to a magnetic field, though most so weakly that we never notice. In this part we describe that response with magnetisation, magnetic intensity and susceptibility, sort materials into diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic, and see how temperature changes their behaviour, including why a hot iron nail stops sticking to a magnet.

slides.heading: Magnetisation, intensity, susceptibility
slides.body_md:
**Magnetisation** $\vec M$: net magnetic moment per unit volume (A m$^{-1}$). For a material in an applied field:
$$\vec B = \mu_0(\vec H + \vec M),\qquad \vec M = \chi\vec H,\qquad \vec B = \mu_0\mu_r\vec H,\qquad \mu_r = 1 + \chi$$
$\vec H$ (**magnetic intensity**, A m$^{-1}$) is set by the free currents, e.g. $H = nI$ in a solenoid.

visual.alt: Table of magnetisation, magnetic intensity, susceptibility and relative permeability with symbols, units and meanings

slides.narration: A material placed in a field becomes magnetised: its atoms’ tiny moments add up to a net moment per unit volume, the magnetisation M. The field from free currents, such as the turns of a solenoid, is described by the magnetic intensity H. For most materials M is proportional to H, and the constant is the susceptibility chi. The total field is mu nought times H plus M, which is mu nought mu r H, with mu r equal to one plus chi.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: magnetisation of a bar
slides.body_md: An iron bar 10 cm × 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm has a magnetic moment of 8.0 A m². Find its magnetisation.
bullets: Step 1 — volume $V = 0.10 \times 0.010 \times 0.010 = 1.0 \times 10^{-5}$ m³.
Comment — a strongly magnetised ferromagnet; the same volume of a paramagnet in a lab field would have M millions of times smaller.

visual.alt: Worked table: a volume of ten to the minus five cubic metre and a moment of 8 ampere square metre give a magnetisation of 8 times ten to the five amperes per metre

slides.narration: Find the volume in cubic metres first: one times ten to the minus five. Divide the magnetic moment by the volume to get the magnetisation, eight times ten to the five amperes per metre. This is typical of a magnetised piece of iron. A paramagnetic material in an ordinary laboratory field would show a magnetisation millions of times smaller.

slides.heading: Three kinds of magnetic material
slides.body_md: In a uniform field, field lines are pushed out of a **diamagnetic** sample, drawn slightly into a **paramagnetic** one and strongly into a **ferromagnetic** one.

visual.alt: Field lines through diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic samples
visual.caption: Exact field of a long cylinder of relative permeability 0.6, 1.5 and 30 in a uniform field.

slides.narration: The three figures show the same uniform field with three different samples placed in it. Lines spread out round the diamagnetic sample, so the field inside is weaker. They crowd a little into the paramagnetic sample and very strongly into the ferromagnetic one, where the field inside is much larger than outside. These pictures come from the exact calculation for a long cylinder.

slides.heading: Diamagnetism
slides.body_md: Diamagnetic materials are **weakly magnetised opposite** to the applied field: $\chi$ small and **negative**, $\mu_r$ slightly less than 1.
bullets: Cause: the field changes the orbital motion of electrons so that the induced moments **oppose** it (all materials show this; it is masked when stronger effects exist).
Examples: bismuth, copper, lead, silicon, water, nitrogen gas, sodium chloride.
Move from stronger to **weaker** field regions; a diamagnetic rod sets **perpendicular** to the field.
Superconductors are perfect diamagnets ($\chi = -1$): they expel the field completely (Meissner effect) — used in maglev trains.

visual.alt: Field lines through diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic samples
visual.caption: Exact field of a long cylinder of relative permeability 0.6, 1.5 and 30 in a uniform field.

slides.narration: In a diamagnetic material the atoms have no net moment of their own. An applied field slightly alters the electrons’ orbits, producing small moments that oppose the field. So chi is small and negative, and the sample is gently pushed towards weaker parts of a field. Bismuth, copper and water behave like this. A superconductor is the extreme case: it expels the field entirely and can float above a magnet.

slides.heading: Paramagnetism
slides.body_md: Paramagnetic materials are **weakly magnetised along** the field: $\chi$ small and **positive**, $\mu_r$ slightly more than 1.
bullets: Cause: atoms have **permanent** magnetic moments; the field partly lines them up, while thermal motion keeps them random.
Examples: aluminium, sodium, calcium, oxygen gas, copper chloride.
Move from weaker to **stronger** field regions; a paramagnetic rod sets **along** the field.
Effect of temperature (Curie law): $\chi = \dfrac{C}{T}$ — cooling makes alignment easier.

visual.alt: Susceptibility of a paramagnet against absolute temperature, falling as one over T: halving the temperature doubles the susceptibility
visual.caption: Curie law: χ ∝ 1/T.

slides.narration: In a paramagnetic material each atom already has a small magnetic moment, but thermal jostling points them in random directions. An applied field lines them up slightly, giving a small magnetisation along the field, so chi is small and positive. Such materials are gently pulled into stronger fields. Because heat fights the alignment, the susceptibility falls as the temperature rises: Curie’s law says chi equals C over T.

slides.heading: Quick check: classify the material
slides.body_md: Use the sign and size of the susceptibility.
slides.narration: Negative susceptibility means diamagnetic; small positive means paramagnetic; very large positive means ferromagnetic.

slides.heading: Ferromagnetism and domains
slides.body_md: Ferromagnetic materials are **strongly magnetised** along the field: $\chi$ and $\mu_r$ very large (hundreds to many thousands).
bullets: Atomic moments line up spontaneously in small regions called **domains** (about 1 mm or less).
Unmagnetised: domains point randomly. In a field, favourable domains grow and others rotate, so the sample becomes strongly magnetised.
Examples: iron, cobalt, nickel, gadolinium and alloys such as alnico.
**Soft** ferromagnets (soft iron) lose magnetisation easily — electromagnet cores; **hard** ones (steel, alnico) retain it — permanent magnets.

slides.narration: In iron, cobalt and nickel, neighbouring atomic moments line up with each other spontaneously, forming domains, each one fully magnetised. In an ordinary piece of iron the domains point every which way and cancel. Put it in a field and the domains pointing along the field grow while others turn, so the whole sample becomes strongly magnetised. Soft iron loses this easily; steel keeps it, making a permanent magnet.

slides.heading: Comparing the three classes
slides.body_md: Quick comparison:
columns:
**Diamagnetic**

- χ: small, negative (about −10⁻⁵)
- μr: slightly < 1
- Moves to weaker field
- Little change with temperature

**Paramagnetic**

- χ: small, positive (10⁻⁵ to 10⁻³)
- μr: slightly > 1
- Moves to stronger field
- χ = C/T

**Ferromagnetic**

- χ: very large, positive (10² to 10⁵)
- μr: ≫ 1
- Strongly attracted into strong fields
- Becomes paramagnetic above the Curie temperature

visual.alt: Table of typical susceptibilities: bismuth about minus 1.7 times ten to the minus five, aluminium about plus 2.3 times ten to the minus five, iron about a thousand to a hundred thousand

slides.narration: The susceptibility sorts the three classes. Diamagnets have a tiny negative chi and are pushed to weaker fields. Paramagnets have a tiny positive chi, are pulled gently into stronger fields, and follow Curie’s law. Ferromagnets have an enormous positive chi and are pulled in strongly, until they are heated above their Curie temperature, when they become paramagnetic.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: an iron-cored solenoid
slides.body_md: A long solenoid has 1000 turns per metre and carries 2.0 A. Its core is iron with $\mu_r = 500$. Find $H$, $B$ in the core, and the magnetisation $M$.
bullets: Step 1 — $H = nI = 1000 \times 2.0 = 2000$ A m$^{-1}$ (set by the current alone).
Step 2 — $B = \mu_0\mu_r H = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 500 \times 2000 \approx 1.26$ T.
Step 3 — $M = (\mu_r - 1)H = 499 \times 2000 \approx 9.98 \times 10^{5}$ A m$^{-1}$.
Comment — without the core $B$ would be only about 2.5 mT: the iron multiplies it 500 times.

slides.narration: H depends only on the free current: one thousand turns per metre times two amperes is two thousand amperes per metre. With iron of relative permeability five hundred, B is mu nought times five hundred times two thousand, about one point two six tesla. The magnetisation is mu r minus one times H, about a million amperes per metre. This is why electromagnets always have iron cores.

slides.heading: Materials in a non-uniform field
slides.body_md: The response is easy to see in a non-uniform field:
bullets: A **paramagnetic** liquid (copper chloride solution) in one arm of a U-tube placed between magnet poles **rises** into the strong field.
A **diamagnetic** liquid (water) in the same set-up is **depressed** slightly.
A small rod hung between the poles sets **along** the field if para- or ferromagnetic, **across** it if diamagnetic.

visual.alt: Field lines through diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic samples
visual.caption: Exact field of a long cylinder of relative permeability 0.6, 1.5 and 30 in a uniform field.

slides.narration: Put a little liquid in a U-tube with one arm between the poles of a strong magnet. A paramagnetic solution, such as copper chloride, creeps up into the strong field. Water, which is diamagnetic, is pushed down very slightly. Hang a small rod between the poles and it turns along the field if it is paramagnetic or ferromagnetic, but across the field if it is diamagnetic.

slides.heading: Quick check: the U-tube
slides.body_md: Predict what happens to the liquid level.
slides.narration: Ask whether the liquid is attracted into or pushed out of the strong field, based on the sign of its susceptibility.

slides.heading: Effect of temperature
slides.body_md: Temperature fights the alignment of atomic moments:
bullets: Diamagnetism: almost independent of temperature.
Paramagnetism: $\chi = C/T$ (Curie law).
Ferromagnetism: above the **Curie temperature** $T_C$ the domains break up and the material becomes paramagnetic (iron: about 1043 K; nickel: about 631 K).

visual.alt: Spontaneous magnetisation of a ferromagnet falling to zero at the Curie temperature, above which the material is only paramagnetic
visual.caption: Shape only: the domains disappear at T_C.

slides.narration: Heating shakes the atomic moments about. Diamagnetism hardly notices, because it does not rely on aligning permanent moments. Paramagnetic susceptibility falls in proportion to one over the absolute temperature. A ferromagnet keeps its domains only below its Curie temperature: above it, alignment is lost and it becomes merely paramagnetic. Heat a magnetised iron nail red-hot and it stops sticking to a magnet.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: using Curie’s law
slides.body_md: A paramagnetic salt has $\chi = 3.0 \times 10^{-4}$ at 300 K. Find its susceptibility at 150 K and at 600 K.
bullets: Step 1 — $\chi T$ is constant: $\chi T = 3.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 300 = 0.09$ K.

visual.alt: Susceptibility of a paramagnet against absolute temperature, falling as one over T: halving the temperature doubles the susceptibility
visual.caption: Curie law: χ ∝ 1/T.

slides.narration: Curie’s law says chi times the absolute temperature stays constant, here zero point zero nine kelvin. Halving the temperature to one hundred and fifty kelvin doubles the susceptibility to six times ten to the minus four. Doubling it to six hundred kelvin halves it to one point five times ten to the minus four. Always use kelvin, never degrees Celsius, in Curie’s law.

slides.heading: Quick check: heating a ferromagnet
slides.body_md: Choose what happens above the Curie temperature.

visual.alt: Spontaneous magnetisation of a ferromagnet falling to zero at the Curie temperature, above which the material is only paramagnetic
visual.caption: Shape only: the domains disappear at T_C.

slides.narration: Think about what happens to the domains when thermal motion becomes strong enough.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 2
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: χ small, negative; pushed to weaker field
χ very large; domains; paramagnetic above $T_C$

visual.alt: Summary table of the field in a material, susceptibility and the three classes of magnetic material

slides.narration: To sum up: a material in a field acquires a magnetisation M, and the total field is mu nought times H plus M. The susceptibility chi, M over H, classifies materials: small and negative for diamagnets, small and positive for paramagnets, and enormous for ferromagnets, which owe their strength to domains. Paramagnetic chi falls as one over T, and a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic above its Curie temperature.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 2
bullets: Give **examples** for each class; examiners expect at least two.
Use kelvin in Curie’s law; $\chi T$ is constant.
$H$ depends on free currents only ($nI$); $B$ and $M$ depend on the material.
Explain ferromagnetism with domains, and the Curie temperature as the loss of domain alignment.

rows: Why χ of paramagnet falls with T
Why iron loses magnetism when hot

visual.alt: Table of common questions and the key point for each

slides.narration: Always give examples when you classify materials. In Curie’s law use absolute temperature, and remember chi times T is constant. Keep H and B apart: H comes only from the free currents, while B and M depend on the material inside. When asked about ferromagnetism or the Curie temperature, explain in terms of domains.

notes.title: Magnetism and Matter — Notes

sections.heading: 1. The bar magnet and its field lines
sections.body_md:
- A freely suspended bar magnet points roughly north–south; its ends are the N and S poles. Like poles repel, unlike attract.
- Poles always occur in pairs: breaking a magnet gives two complete magnets. **No magnetic monopoles** have been found.
- **Field lines** are continuous **closed loops**: outside N → S, inside S → N. They never cross; crowding shows strength; the tangent gives the direction of $\vec B$.
- Because lines never start or end, the net magnetic flux through any closed surface is zero.
- Electric field lines of a dipole start on + and end on −; magnetic lines have no ends.

key_terms.definition_md: A closed curve whose tangent gives the direction of the magnetic field.
An isolated N or S pole; none has been observed.

sections.heading: 2. The bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid
sections.body_md:
A current-carrying solenoid produces the same field pattern as a bar magnet (qualitative treatment). Its magnetic moment is $m = NIA$, directed along the axis towards the end where the current appears anticlockwise (the N end).

Inside a magnet, the orbital and spin motion of electrons in its atoms act like tiny aligned current loops; their moments add up to the magnet’s moment $\vec m$ (from S to N, unit A m²).

Cutting a solenoid in half gives two shorter solenoids, each with N and S ends — the same as breaking a magnet.

sections.heading: 3. Magnetic dipole: field and torque (qualitative)
sections.body_md:
**Field** (far away, by analogy with the electric dipole):
- axial point: along $\vec m$, $\propto \dfrac{2m}{r^3}$;
- equatorial point: opposite to $\vec m$, $\propto \dfrac{m}{r^3}$ — half the axial value at the same $r$.

**In a uniform field:** net force zero; torque $\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B$ ($\tau = mB\sin\theta$) turns the magnet into line with $\vec B$. Stable equilibrium when $\vec m \parallel \vec B$ (energy $-mB$), unstable when antiparallel ($+mB$). A slightly displaced magnet oscillates about the field direction — the basis of the compass needle.

| | Electric dipole | Magnetic dipole |
|---|---|---|
| Moment | $\vec p$ (C m) | $\vec m$ (A m²) |
| Torque | $\vec p \times \vec E$ | $\vec m \times \vec B$ |
| Far field | $\propto p/r^3$ | $\propto m/r^3$ |

sections.heading: 4. Magnetisation and the magnetic quantities
sections.body_md:
- **Magnetisation** $M$: net magnetic moment per unit volume, A m$^{-1}$.
- **Magnetic intensity** $H$: set by free currents (e.g. $H = nI$ in a solenoid), A m$^{-1}$.
- $\vec B = \mu_0(\vec H + \vec M)$; for linear materials $\vec M = \chi\vec H$, so $\vec B = \mu_0\mu_r\vec H$ with $\mu_r = 1 + \chi$ and permeability $\mu = \mu_0\mu_r$.
- $\chi$ and $\mu_r$ have no units.

*Worked result:* an iron core with $\mu_r = 500$ in a solenoid with $H = 2000$ A m$^{-1}$ gives $B \approx 1.26$ T and $M \approx 1.0 \times 10^{6}$ A m$^{-1}$.

key_terms.definition_md: Net magnetic moment per unit volume of a material.
χ = M/H; measures how readily a material is magnetised.

sections.heading: 5. Dia-, para- and ferromagnetism
sections.body_md:
| | Diamagnetic | Paramagnetic | Ferromagnetic |
|---|---|---|---|
| χ | small, negative (≈ −10⁻⁵) | small, positive (10⁻⁵–10⁻³) | very large (10²–10⁵) |
| μr | slightly < 1 | slightly > 1 | ≫ 1 |
| Atomic moments | none (induced, opposing) | permanent, randomly oriented | permanent, aligned in domains |
| In a non-uniform field | moves to weaker field | moves to stronger field | strongly attracted |
| Rod between poles | sets across the field | sets along the field | sets along the field |
| Examples | Bi, Cu, Pb, water, N₂, NaCl | Al, Na, Ca, O₂, CuCl₂ | Fe, Co, Ni, Gd, alnico |

- Superconductors are perfect diamagnets ($\chi = -1$, Meissner effect).
- **Domains:** regions in which atomic moments are spontaneously aligned. In a field, favourably aligned domains grow and others rotate.
- **Soft** ferromagnets (soft iron) magnetise and demagnetise easily — electromagnet and transformer cores. **Hard** ferromagnets (steel, alnico) retain magnetisation — permanent magnets.

key_terms.definition_md: A small region of a ferromagnet in which all atomic moments are aligned.
Complete expulsion of a magnetic field from a superconductor.

sections.heading: 6. Effect of temperature
sections.body_md:
- **Diamagnetism:** nearly independent of temperature.
- **Paramagnetism:** Curie law $\chi = \dfrac{C}{T}$ ($T$ in kelvin): thermal agitation opposes alignment, so χ falls as T rises; $\chi T$ is constant.
- **Ferromagnetism:** above the **Curie temperature** $T_C$ the domain alignment is destroyed and the material becomes paramagnetic (Fe ≈ 1043 K, Ni ≈ 631 K, Co ≈ 1394 K). A heated magnet loses its magnetism.

key_terms.definition_md: Temperature above which a ferromagnet becomes paramagnetic.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Magnetic field lines of a bar magnet start on its north pole and end on its south pole, just as electric field lines start on positive and end on negative charges.
questions.solution_md: False. Magnetic field lines have no ends: outside the magnet they run from N to S, and they continue inside from S to N, forming closed loops.

questions.stem_md: A bar magnet is broken into three equal pieces. Each piece

options.text_md: has only a north pole or only a south pole
is a complete magnet with its own north and south poles
is unmagnetised except the two end pieces
has a north pole at both ends

questions.solution_md: Magnetic poles always come in pairs; isolated poles are not found — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Inside a bar magnet, the magnetic field lines run

options.text_md: from the north pole to the south pole
nowhere: the field inside is zero
from the south pole to the north pole
perpendicular to the length of the magnet

questions.solution_md: The lines are closed loops: N → S outside, so S → N inside — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A closed surface is drawn round the north-pole end of a bar magnet only (the surface cuts through the magnet). The net magnetic flux out of this surface is

options.text_md: positive, because field lines leave the north pole
negative, because field lines enter the north pole
equal to μ₀ times the pole strength

questions.solution_md: Field lines are closed loops: every line leaving the surface outside re-enters it through the part that cuts the magnet, so the net flux is zero — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A solenoid of 250 turns, each of area 4.0 cm², carries 2.0 A. Find its magnetic moment, in A m².
questions.solution_md: $m = NIA = 250 \times 2.0 \times 4.0 \times 10^{-4} = 0.20$ A m².

questions.stem_md: Looking at one end of a current-carrying solenoid from outside, you see the current flowing anticlockwise. That end behaves like

options.text_md: neither pole, since a solenoid has no poles
a north pole only if the solenoid has an iron core

questions.solution_md: By the right-hand rule the field at that end points towards you, out of the solenoid, so it is a north pole — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A long solenoid with magnetic moment $m$ is cut into two equal halves; each half keeps the same current and the same turn area. The magnetic moment of each half is
questions.solution_md: Each half has half the turns, and $m = NIA$, so each has $m/2$ — just as each half of a broken bar magnet is a weaker complete magnet — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which property is true of magnetic field lines but NOT of electrostatic field lines?

options.text_md: Their crowding shows the field strength
Their tangent gives the direction of the field

questions.solution_md: The other three are true of both; electrostatic lines begin and end on charges, magnetic lines never end — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A current-carrying solenoid behaves like a bar magnet.

**Reason (R):** Each turn of the solenoid acts as a small magnetic dipole, and the moments of all the turns add along the axis.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true; the aligned moments of the turns add up to a net moment $NIA$ along the axis, giving the bar-magnet pattern — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A magnetic field line can begin on a north pole and end there on a nearby south pole.

**Reason (R):** Isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) have not been found.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: magnetic field lines never begin or end; they continue through the magnet and form closed loops — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Two magnetic field lines can never intersect.
questions.solution_md: True. At an intersection the field would have two directions at one point.

questions.stem_md: Describe how you would trace the field lines of a bar magnet on a sheet of paper using a small plotting compass, and say how the result shows that the lines run from N to S outside the magnet.

answer.model_answer_md: Put the compass near the **N pole** and dot both ends of its needle. Move it so its tail is on the head dot, dot again, repeat, and join the dots. The needle’s north end always points **away from N, towards S**, so the lines run from N to S outside.

questions.solution_md: Step the compass along its own direction.

marking_scheme.step: Method: mark needle ends and step along, join dots
Needle north end shows direction N → S outside

questions.stem_md: Give two observations that show that a current-carrying solenoid is equivalent to a bar magnet.

answer.model_answer_md: A freely suspended solenoid carrying current **sets north–south** like a magnet, and its ends **attract and repel** the poles of a bar magnet just as poles do. questions.stem_md: A magnetised iron nail is heated in a flame until it glows red, and then it no longer attracts small pins. Explain why.

answer.model_answer_md: Iron is ferromagnetic only below its **Curie temperature** (about 1043 K, which red heat reaches). Heating gives the atoms so much **thermal energy** that the alignment within the **domains** is destroyed, so the nail loses its magnetisation and becomes merely **paramagnetic**, too weak to attract the pins.

questions.solution_md: Domains destroyed above the Curie temperature.

questions.stem_md: Two U-tubes contain water and a copper chloride solution, each with one arm between the poles of a strong magnet. Predict what happens to the liquid levels and explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Copper chloride solution is **paramagnetic**: it is pulled into the stronger field, so its level **rises** slightly in the arm between the poles. Water is **diamagnetic**: it is pushed towards the weaker field, so its level **falls** very slightly in that arm.

questions.solution_md: Para moves to stronger field; dia to weaker.

questions.stem_md: Explain why a small magnet can float above a superconductor cooled below its critical temperature.

answer.model_answer_md: Below its critical temperature the superconductor **expels the magnetic field** (Meissner effect): it is a **perfect diamagnet** with χ = −1. Currents on its surface create a field that **opposes** the magnet’s field, so the magnet is **repelled**; it floats where this repulsion balances its weight.

questions.solution_md: Perfect diamagnetism repels the magnet.

questions.stem_md: Explain, using domains, why a piece of iron is strongly magnetised in a field although an ordinary piece of iron is not a magnet.

answer.model_answer_md: Iron consists of tiny **domains**, in each of which the atomic moments are **spontaneously aligned**, so each domain is strongly magnetised. In an ordinary piece the domains point in **random** directions and their moments **cancel**, so there is no net magnetisation. In an applied field, domains aligned with the field **grow** at the expense of others and other domains **rotate** towards the field, so their moments add and the iron becomes **strongly magnetised**.

questions.solution_md: Random domains cancel; a field grows and rotates them.

marking_scheme.step: Random orientation cancels in unmagnetised iron
Field: domain growth and rotation give strong magnetisation

(b) **Dia:** χ small and negative, almost independent of temperature. **Para:** χ small and positive, falling with temperature, χ = C/T.
(c) **Dia:** move towards weaker field. **Para:** move towards stronger field.

questions.stem_md: (a) Explain why a bar magnet is said to be equivalent to a current-carrying solenoid, and draw (describe) the field lines of both. (b) A solenoid of 500 turns, each of area 3.0 cm², carries 1.2 A. Find its magnetic moment. (c) How does the far field of this solenoid change if (i) the distance is doubled along its axis, (ii) the point is moved to the equatorial line at the same distance?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A solenoid carrying current produces a field identical in pattern to that of a bar magnet: closed loops that emerge from one end (N), curve round outside and enter the other end (S), continuing inside from S to N. Both have poles that cannot be separated, both set north–south when suspended, and both attract and repel other magnets in the same way. In a magnet, the electrons in the atoms act like tiny aligned current loops, so the magnet behaves as a solenoid with moment $m = NIA$.

(b) $m = NIA = 500 \times 1.2 \times 3.0 \times 10^{-4} = 0.18$ A m², along the axis towards the N end.

(c)(i) The far field varies as $1/r^3$: doubling the distance makes it **8 times weaker**. (ii) At the same distance on the equatorial line it is **half** the axial value and points **opposite** to $\vec m$.

questions.solution_md: Compare the field patterns; m = NIA; dipole ratios.

questions.stem_md: (a) A bar magnet of moment $\vec m$ lies at angle θ to a uniform field $\vec B$. Explain why it experiences a torque but no net force, and state the torque. (b) Describe its stable and unstable equilibrium positions in terms of its potential energy. (c) A magnet of moment 0.40 A m² is in a uniform field of 0.25 T. Find the torque when θ = 30°, and the work needed to turn it from θ = 0° to θ = 180°.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In the pole picture, the N pole is pushed along $\vec B$ and the S pole against it with equal forces: the **net force is zero**. The two forces act along different lines, forming a **couple**, so there is a torque $\vec\tau = \vec m \times \vec B$, of size $mB\sin\theta$, which turns the magnet towards the field.

(b) The potential energy is $U = -mB\cos\theta$. **Stable:** $\theta = 0^\circ$, $U = -mB$ (minimum) — a small turn produces a restoring torque. **Unstable:** $\theta = 180^\circ$, $U = +mB$ (maximum) — a small turn produces a torque that turns it further away.

(c) $\tau = mB\sin 30^\circ = 0.40 \times 0.25 \times 0.5 = 0.050$ N m. Work $W = U(180^\circ) - U(0^\circ) = 2mB = 2 \times 0.40 \times 0.25 = 0.20$ J.

questions.solution_md: Couple from equal and opposite pole forces; U = −mB cos θ.

marking_scheme.step: τ = mB sin θ = m × B
Stable and unstable positions with energies

questions.stem_md: (a) Define magnetisation M, magnetic intensity H and magnetic susceptibility χ. (b) Starting from $B = \mu_0(H + M)$, show that $\mu_r = 1 + \chi$. (c) A long solenoid with 1500 turns per metre carries 2.0 A and is filled with a material of susceptibility 299. Find H, M and B in the material.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **M:** net magnetic moment per unit volume of the material (A m$^{-1}$). **H:** the magnetic intensity set up by the free (conduction) currents, e.g. $nI$ in a solenoid (A m$^{-1}$). **χ:** the ratio $M/H$ for a linear material (no unit).

(b) $B = \mu_0(H + M) = \mu_0(H + \chi H) = \mu_0(1 + \chi)H$. Writing $B = \mu_0\mu_r H$ gives $\mu_r = 1 + \chi$.

(c) $H = nI = 1500 \times 2.0 = 3000$ A m$^{-1}$; $M = \chi H = 299 \times 3000 = 897000$ A m$^{-1}$; $B = \mu_0(1 + \chi)H = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 300 \times 3000 \approx 1.13$ T.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; substitute M = χH; then numbers.

questions.stem_md: Compare diamagnetic, paramagnetic and ferromagnetic materials under the headings: (a) atomic origin of magnetism, (b) susceptibility and relative permeability, (c) behaviour in a non-uniform magnetic field, (d) effect of temperature. Give two examples of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Dia:** no permanent atomic moments; the applied field induces opposing moments. **Para:** permanent atomic moments, randomly oriented; the field partly aligns them. **Ferro:** permanent moments aligned spontaneously within **domains**.

(b) **Dia:** χ small, negative; μr slightly < 1. **Para:** χ small, positive; μr slightly > 1. **Ferro:** χ and μr very large (hundreds to thousands).

(c) **Dia:** move towards weaker field; a rod sets across the field. **Para:** move towards stronger field; a rod sets along it. **Ferro:** strongly pulled into strong fields.

(d) **Dia:** almost unaffected. **Para:** χ = C/T (Curie law). **Ferro:** become paramagnetic above the Curie temperature.

Examples — dia: bismuth, copper; para: aluminium, sodium; ferro: iron, nickel.

questions.stem_md: An engineer must choose materials for (i) the core of an electromagnet for a door lock that must release instantly when the power is cut, and (ii) a permanent magnet for a bicycle dynamo. (a) Explain, using domains, what property each material needs. (b) Name a suitable material for each. (c) Explain why both magnets would fail if they were run very hot, above the Curie temperature of their materials. (d) Why is copper unsuitable for either?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) The lock core must be **strongly magnetised** while the current flows (high permeability) and lose its magnetisation **immediately** when it stops: its domains must realign easily and fall back to random orientation (a **soft** ferromagnet). (ii) The dynamo magnet must **keep** its magnetisation with no current: its domains, once aligned, must resist being disturbed (a **hard** ferromagnet).

(b) (i) **Soft iron**. (ii) **Steel** or **alnico**.

(c) Above the Curie temperature thermal agitation destroys the alignment within the domains; both materials become merely **paramagnetic**, so the lock would hold only weakly and the dynamo magnet would lose its magnetism.

(d) Copper is **diamagnetic** (χ tiny and negative): it cannot be magnetised strongly at all.

questions.solution_md: Soft vs hard ferromagnets; Curie temperature; copper is diamagnetic.

questions.passage_md: A student uses a smartphone magnetometer app to measure the field of a small bar magnet in a room in Jaipur, far from other magnets. answer.model_answer_md:

**(b)** 25 μT

**(c)** (i) The field on the equatorial line points **opposite to the magnetic moment**, i.e. parallel to the magnet’s axis but from its **N end towards its S end**. This matches the field lines, which run outside the magnet from N round to S.

questions.passage_md: In a science exhibition in Chennai, a small disc of a high-temperature superconductor is cooled with liquid nitrogen (77 K). A small neodymium magnet placed above it floats steadily in mid-air. When the disc warms up above its critical temperature, the magnet drops onto it.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) a perfect diamagnet, with χ = −1

**(b)** (b) zero

**(c)** (i) While cold, the superconductor **expels** the magnet’s field: currents on its surface produce a field opposing the magnet’s, so the magnet is **repelled** and floats where the repulsion balances its weight. Above the critical temperature the material is no longer superconducting; it is only weakly magnetic, the repulsion **disappears** and the magnet falls.

**OR** (ii) The suggestion is **wrong** in practice. Copper is diamagnetic, but its χ is only about **−10⁻⁵**, so the repulsive force is about **100 000 times** weaker than for a superconductor (χ = −1) — far too small to support the magnet’s weight.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** It expels the magnetic field completely (Meissner effect): χ = −1 — option (d).

**(b)** With χ = −1, M = −H and B = μ₀(H + M) = 0 — option (b).

**(c)** (i) Repulsion by perfect diamagnetism; lost above the critical temperature.

(ii) Compare the size of χ.

options.text_md: a paramagnet obeying the Curie law

children.solution_md: It expels the magnetic field completely (Meissner effect): χ = −1 — option (d).

options.text_md: equal to the field of the magnet

children.solution_md: With χ = −1, M = −H and B = μ₀(H + M) = 0 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Small rods of aluminium and of bismuth are hung in turn between the flat poles of a strong magnet. Predict how each sets and explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Aluminium is **paramagnetic**: its ends are drawn towards the stronger field near the poles, so the rod sets **along** the field. Bismuth is **diamagnetic**: its ends are pushed towards the weaker field away from the poles, so the rod sets **across** the field.

questions.solution_md: Para moves to stronger field, dia to weaker.

questions.stem_md: A bar magnet of moment 0.24 A m² is to be replaced by an equivalent solenoid whose turns have area 2.0 cm² and carry 1.2 A. How many turns are needed?
questions.solution_md: $N = \dfrac{m}{IA} = \dfrac{0.24}{1.2 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-4}} = 1000$ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Two identical bar magnets lie on one straight line with their north poles facing each other a short distance apart. At the point midway between the two north poles, the magnetic field due to the magnets is

options.text_md: twice the field of one magnet
directed towards one of the magnets
perpendicular to the line of the magnets

questions.solution_md: By symmetry the two magnets give equal fields in opposite directions at the midpoint (each points away from its own north pole), so they cancel — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Ignoring the Earth’s field, a small compass is placed on the equatorial line of a bar magnet, some distance from it. The north end of the compass needle points

options.text_md: parallel to the magnet, in the direction from the magnet’s N end towards its S end
parallel to the magnet, in the direction from its S end towards its N end
straight towards the centre of the magnet

questions.solution_md: The needle lines up with $\vec B$. On the equatorial line $\vec B$ is opposite to $\vec m$ (which points S → N), i.e. it points from the N end towards the S end — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In an iron core, the magnetic field is 0.88 T when the magnetic intensity is 1000 A m⁻¹. Find the relative permeability of the iron (to the nearest 10).
questions.solution_md: $\mu_r = \dfrac{B}{\mu_0 H} = \dfrac{0.88}{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 1000} \approx 700$, i.e. about 700.

questions.stem_md: A paramagnetic salt has susceptibility χ at 27 °C. Its susceptibility at −73 °C is

options.text_md: χ, because the Curie law needs kelvin

questions.solution_md: Use kelvin: 300 K and 200 K. $\chi T$ is constant, so the new value is $\chi \times 300/200 = 1.5\chi$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A nickel ball hangs from a thread so that it is pulled sideways by a magnet. When the ball is heated to about 360 °C it swings back and hangs vertically; on cooling it is pulled again. The best explanation is that at about 360 °C nickel

options.text_md: passes its Curie temperature and becomes only paramagnetic

questions.solution_md: Nickel’s Curie temperature is about 631 K (358 °C). Above it the domains break up and the attraction becomes very weak; below it they re-form on cooling — option (a).
